Topics Countries Explainer About Contributors The Quarterly Submissions Search Northeast Asia Geopolitics is prolonging China’s overcapacity problem Published: 24 October 2026 Reading Time: 5 mins Back Authors Patrick Xue The Australian National University Back In Brief Rather than forcing unviable Chinese plants to close, Western tariffs, supply chain securitisation and investment screening risk prolonging excess capacity while encouraging costly duplicate production abroad. Addressing this imbalance requires pairing China’s domestic restructuring with more open trade and investment, allowing competitive firms to meet global demand while uneconomic capacity exits. Without such adjustment, geopolitical measures may simply shift overcapacity across borders rather than resolve it.
Listen to this article Western governments’ are making increasing use of a geopolitical toolkit of tariffs, supply chain securitisation and investment screening in response to Chinese industrial overcapacity. But together, these policies risks prolonging, rather than resolving, China’s overcapacity problem — at a rising cost to themselves.
Overcapacity generally eases when firms reach markets that can absorb their surplus output through exports or relocation, or close commercially unviable plants. Ideally, the least competitive firms would exit wherever they are located, not only in China. Yet today’s geopolitical toolkit obstructs market adjustments while adding to global supply. Tariffs restrict export access without reliably forcing closures. Securitised supply chains keep unviable plants operating and duplicate capacity elsewhere. Investment screening blocks relocation to markets with genuine demand .
While tariffs can squeeze exporters’ margins and push firms towards closure, firms may redirect sales, move final processing offshore or produce abroad where markets remain accessible. For capital-intensive Chinese firms, closure threatens debt repayment and local jobs, incentivising lenders and local governments to keep supporting production. When cheap credit or subsidies keep otherwise unviable plants operating, lost export sales do not automatically translate into market exit. At the same time, these tariffs shelter producers in importing markets from restructuring.
Securitised framing of supply chains not only discourages closure of inefficient plants but encourages new capacity on both sides. When Western restrictions aimed at reducing dependence on China are seen by Beijing as economic containment, China’s push for self-sufficiency further reinforces Western fears, creating a security dilemma as illustrated by China’s rare earth export restrictions . For individual countries, spare capacity provides insurance against disruptions. Collectively, these insurance premiums manifest as duplicated global capacity that is shielded from market-driven forces.
As investment screening increasingly targets ownership and control, local production may no longer secure market access, obstructing cross-border restructuring. Under the US ‘ connected vehicle ’ rule, starting from model year 2027, Chinese-controlled manufacturers face sales restrictions — even for US-made vehicles — unless they obtain authorisation. This reflects concerns that local production cannot resolve security risks involving data access and corporate control. The European Union, despite imposing Chinese 2024 electric vehicle (EV) duties in 2024, has kept this route open. BYD began trial production in Hungary in 2026, though its investments remain under scrutiny over state subsidies.
Japan’s experience shows how trade pressure and foreign investment can jointly prompt industrial adjustment. Voluntary export restraints introduced in 1981 limited shipments from Japanese automakers, but allowed Japanese-owned factories to supply US consumers through local production. Because localisation substituted for exports rather than supplementing them, Japan’s domestic vehicle output peaked in 1990 before declining as overseas production grew. While China lacks Japan’s strategic alliance with the United States, product-level restrictions can still apply where security risks are limited.
But when trade and security restrictions operate together, the option of replacing exports with local production grows less viable. Even where possible, localisation reduces overcapacity only if it replaces capacity at home, displaces capacity that would otherwise be built or meets new demand.
Global excess steelmaking capacity, for example, reached around 26 per cent of total capacity in 2025. With high-income markets increasingly restricted and new blast-furnace capacity capped at home, Chinese steelmakers are building abroad. Cross-border investments account for roughly 21 per cent of planned steelmaking capacity from 2025 onward, with Chinese firms involved in more than half of that capacity — mostly in blast furnace-basic oxygen furnace configurations with economic lives spanning decades. Redirecting investment overseas risks locking in rather than resolving excess capacity.
None of this relieves China of its own policy homework. Ending support for unviable plants, restructuring debt and assisting displaced workers would ease fiscal and credit burdens, while stronger domestic demand would also help absorb output. But that adjustment is made politically harder when other governments subsidise or protect their own capacity, as Washington and Brussels do in batteries, EVs and solar. Governments need assurance that retiring inefficient plants will not simply surrender markets to publicly supported rivals.
World Trade Organisation trade policy reviews could scrutinise the purpose and effects of these geopolitical tools. Governments disagree over which capabilities require protection and resist external review of national security measures. While this limits binding institutional solutions, it leaves room for dialogue. Governments should shield routine information sharing and technical assessments from geopolitical pressure and apply institutional rules consistently.
Though China exited the G20’s Global Forum on Steel Excess Capacity in 2019, a review that also scrutinises Western security-driven measures could incentivise Beijing’s participation. Reviews could assess whether tariffs close plants or merely divert sales, whether security policies exceed identified needs and whether targeted safeguards could replace blanket ownership restrictions.
Shielding national industries through tariffs, securitised supply chains and investment screening will not resolve China’s overcapacity. A more effective response combines China’s domestic restructuring with open trade and investment, allowing competitive production to reach demand while uneconomic capacity exits.
Former Australian prime minister Kevin Rudd’s ‘ managed strategic competition ’ offers a guiding principle — preserve cooperation where interests overlap within clear strategic guardrails. For overcapacity, this means keeping viable adjustment channels open while seeking reciprocal commitments to withdraw the support sustaining it. Without both, governments risk paying to protect existing plants while subsidising yet more underutilised capacity.
Patrick Xue is Research Scholar at the East Asian Bureau of Economic Research in the Crawford School of Public Policy, The Australian National University.
